text.p: Cloudy skies in Florida forced flight controllers to delay the planned homecoming of space shuttle Columbia on Thursday.
The shuttle's crew of five were 15 minutes away from firing Columbia's braking rockets to begin their descent when mission control called off the planned 7:33 a.m. EST (1233 GMT) landing.

"The clouds around KSC (Kennedy Space Center) are not going to cooperate with us on this particular attempt," spacecraft communicator Curt Brown informed the astronauts. "We are no-go for the deorbit burn."
Forecasters advised against a landing because clouds were moving off the Atlantic Ocean toward the shuttle's landing strip at its Florida base.
Columbia had another landing opportunity at the Kennedy Space Centre at 9:10 a.m. EST (1410 GMT). The shuttle could also be diverted to NASA's backup runway at Edwards Air Force Base in California.
NASA prefers to land the shuttles whenever possible at its Florida to avoid the additional $1 million cost of transporting the shuttle back from California.
Space agency officials ordered Columbia home one day earlier than planned when weather conditions began to worsen at all of the shuttle's landing sites.
The decision to end the mission early also came after a stuck airlock hatch last weekend forced NASA to scrap a pair of planned spacewalks.

Ground controllers closely watched as shuttle astronaut Tammy Jernigan and the rest of the crew closed Columbia's cargo bay doors shortly before 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT). The doors have always operated smoothly on NASA's previous 79 shuttle flights, but had there been a problem the astronauts would have had to pry open the stuck hatch and make a spacewalk to manually crank the doors closed.
During the night, shuttle commander Ken Cockrell tested all 38 steering jets on the orbiter to make sure they were working for the high-speed descent.

The astronauts released and later retrieved two science satellites during their 16-day flight. A U.S.-German telescope studied the life cycles of stars and a prototype computer chip factory manufactured ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry.
